evidence.quote:
The man and woman loved the dog very much; perhaps this was
because it had been such a task to win his love.
evidence.paraphrase: Walt and Madge cherished the dog, partly because winning his affection had been difficult.

evidence.quote:
He was possessed of an obsession that drove him
north.
The homing instinct, Irvine called it
evidence.paraphrase: Irvine explains the dog's repeated flights northward as a homing instinct.

evidence.quote:
Things is different down here,
Miller
explained.

You don
don
t have to eat dogs.
evidence.paraphrase: Miller contrasts the harsh Klondike, where dogs may be eaten, with the mild conditions of California.

evidence.quote:
Walt and Madge stared at each other.
The miracle had
happened.
Wolf had barked.
evidence.paraphrase: Walt and Madge are astonished when the previously silent dog barks upon meeting Miller.

evidence.quote:
He
lifted one of Wolf
s fore legs and examined the foot-pads,
pressing them and denting them with his thumb.
evidence.paraphrase: Miller physically examines the dog's paw pads to assess how long it has been off the trail.

evidence.quote:
He was depressed by the
coldness of these humans who had never been cold before.
evidence.paraphrase: The dog becomes distressed by the unresponsiveness of the humans as he tries to make a choice.
